intro: A clear email in English helps you book things, ask for information, say thank you or say sorry. An English email follows a simple plan and uses fixed phrases. This lesson gives you those phrases, from friendly to formal.
objectifs: Organise an email: subject, greeting, opening, body, closing, sign-off.
Choose the greeting and the sign-off for the situation (Hi Tom / Dear Ms Martin; Best wishes / Kind regards).
Use key phrases: I'm writing to…, Could you…?, I've attached…, I look forward to hearing from you.
Avoid common mistakes (“I write you”, “in attachment”, “Cordially”).

texte: A good email is short and organised. Each part has a job: the subject gives the topic in a few words, the first sentence gives the reason for writing, then come the details and the request, and finally a closing sentence.
In English, put a comma after the greeting (“Dear Anna,”) and start the next sentence with a capital letter on a new line. Leave an empty line between paragraphs, with no indent.

lignes: say hello in the right style
I'm writing to book a room.
We'd like a double room for two nights. Could you…?
I look forward to hearing from you.
Kind regards, / Best wishes, + Amina Diallo
the last words and your name

texte: Formal (a company, an office, someone you don't know): “Dear Mr Lambert,” (man), “Dear Ms Lambert,” (woman, whether married or not), “Dear Sir or Madam,” (name unknown). Finish with “Kind regards,” or “Best regards,”; in a very formal letter, “Yours sincerely,” (name known) or “Yours faithfully,” (UK, name unknown).
Neutral (a colleague, a client you know): “Dear Anna,” or “Hello Anna,”; finish with “Best wishes,” or “Kind regards,”.
Friendly (a friend, family): “Hi Tom,”, “Hey Tom,” (very informal); finish with “See you soon,”, “Love,” (family, close friends), “Cheers,” (UK, informal).

lignes: a manager, a teacher you don't know

sections.note: In British English, “Mr”, “Ms”, “Mrs”, “Dr” have no full stop; in American English they do (Mr., Ms.). Use the family name, never the first name alone after Mr / Ms: “Dear Ms Dubois”, not “Dear Ms Claire”.

texte: To say why you are writing: “I'm writing to…” (+ verb) or “I'm writing about…” (+ noun). This is the present continuous, never “I write you”.
To answer an email: “Thank you for your email.”, “Thanks for your message.” (more informal). To a friend: “I hope you're well.” / “How are you?”
exemples: I'm writing to ask about your English courses.
I'm writing about my order number 4521.
Thank you for your quick reply.
Hi Léa, I hope you're well! Thanks for the photos.

texte: To ask politely: “Could you send me…?”, “Could you tell me…?”, “I'd like to…” (lessons 34 and 57). With “please”: “Please let me know if…”.
For an attachment: “I've attached…” or “Please find attached…” (formal). Don't say “in attachment”.
To say sorry: “Sorry for the late reply.” / “I'm sorry, but I can't come on Friday.”
exemples: Could you send me the price list, please?
Please let me know if you need more information.
Sorry for the late reply. I was on holiday.

texte: Formal: “I look forward to hearing from you.” Careful: “look forward to” takes -ing (“to hearing”, not “to hear”).
Neutral: “Thanks in advance.”, “Let me know if you have any questions.”
exemples: I look forward to hearing from you.
Thanks in advance for your help.
Can't wait to see you! Love, Mariam

formule: Dear Ms… / Hi…, — I'm writing to… — Could you…? / I've attached… — I look forward to hearing from you. — Kind regards, / Best wishes,
prononciation: “attached” /əˈtætʃt/: only two syllables; the -ed sounds like /t/.
To say an address: @ = “at”, . = “dot”, - = “hyphen” or “dash”, _ = “underscore”: anna.diallo@mail.com = “anna dot diallo at mail dot com”.
erreurs: I write you to ask a question.
I'm writing to ask a question.
Fixed phrase in the present continuous, with no “you”.
Please find in attachment my CV.
Please find attached my CV. / I've attached my CV.
Use “attached”.
I wait for your answer.
I look forward to hearing from you.
The polite closing phrase.
I look forward to hear from you.
I look forward to hearing from you.
“Look forward to” + -ing.
Dear Madam Smith,
Dear Ms Smith,
With a name: Ms / Mrs / Mr + family name.
Cordially,
Kind regards, / Best regards,
“Cordially” is not a normal English sign-off.
Hello Mister,
Dear Sir or Madam, / Hello Mr Brown,
Don't use “Mister” alone; Mr + name.
Dear John. I hope you are fine.
Dear John, I hope you're well.
Comma after the greeting; “I hope you're well” is more natural.

dialogue.contexte: In an office in Brussels, Ahmed helps his colleague Julie write an email in English to a hotel in Dublin.
lignes: Ahmed, can you help me? I need to write to a hotel in Dublin.
Sure. Do you know the manager's name?
Then start with “Dear Sir or Madam”. Then say why you're writing.
“I'm writing to book two single rooms for the 3rd and 4th of June.” Is that OK?
Perfect. Now ask your question politely.
“Could you tell me if breakfast is included?”
Great. And finish with “I look forward to hearing from you. Kind regards.”
No, nobody says that! “Kind regards” is perfect.

mots: add a file to an email
a file sent with an email
Can you forward me the email?
send an email you received to another person
good wishes (at the end of an email)
the place where new emails arrive
used at the end of a formal letter
I look forward to meeting you.
feel happy about something that will happen (+ -ing)

items: I look forward to hearing from you.

exercices.consigne: Each phrase has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: I write you to book a table.
I'm writing to book a table.
Please find in attachment the document.
Please find attached the document. / I've attached the document.
I look forward to hear from you.
I look forward to hearing from you.
Thank you for your mail of yesterday.
Thank you for your email yesterday. / Thank you for yesterday's email.

exercices.consigne: Write a formal email (60 to 80 words) to a language school in Toronto to ask about summer courses: dates, prices, accommodation.
items: Subject: Summer English courses. Dear Sir or Madam, I'm writing to ask about your summer English courses. I'm a 24-year-old student from Cameroon and my level is A2. Could you tell me the dates and the price of the July course? I'd also like to know if you can help with accommodation. I've attached my last English test. I look forward to hearing from you. Kind regards, Brice Nkoulou

a_retenir: Plan: subject → greeting → reason (I'm writing to…) → details and request → closing → sign-off.
Formal: Dear Mr / Ms + family name, or Dear Sir or Madam; Kind regards / Yours sincerely / Yours faithfully.
Friendly: Hi + first name; See you soon / Love / Cheers.
Key phrases: Could you…? · I've attached… · Please let me know if… · I look forward to hearing from you (+ -ing).
Never: I write you, in attachment, Cordially, Dear Madam Smith.
